question:
I provide the central question which is the purpose of this post first, followed by the problem context. Please let me know if you want me to clarify anything or require more information.

Question

Why do all bash commands work when running our container with a user that doesn't exist, except for dbt commands which fail silently?

Some people I talked to hypothesize this has to do with permissions. However, if I try to execute another command, such as touch test.py, I get a permission denied error, as expected.

Why is there no output whatsoever when I run dbt commands?

Problem context

Background

I am using an image that I have built to run dbt transformations in my CI/CD pipeline as part of my tests. The docker run command used to work as expected until I added my dbt source code to the container instead of mounting a volume with the CI/CD working directory that includes the source code.

I have managed to solve the issue, but I need help understanding what is going on a bit better.

Running the container that doesn't contain the source code by mounting a volume

Before I added the source code to the container, my working docker run command looked like this:

docker run --rm --env-file .env --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -v "$PWD":"$PWD" -w "$PWD/dbt" "${IMAGE_URI}" bash -c "dbt deps ${CI_PROFILE_TARGET} && dbt seed ${CI_PROFILE_TARGET} ${REFRESH:-"--full-refresh"}"

For anyone who is interested in the details, we do the following things above:

  • We mount the current directory with all the dbt related files to the container.
  • We set the working to directory as $PWD/dbt, which is the directory with the dbt project.
  • We set the user to have the same id and group id as the user running the docker run command.
    • That ensures that the files generated under the working directory can be later deleted by the CI/CD user that runs the container. Note that the working directory is under the mounted volume so anything generated by the container will be available in the CI/CD build in the gitlab runner instance.
  • The specific dbt commands don't really matter in this case, but we basically install the dependencies and create the seed tables.

Silent container failure - First attempt to run container that contains dbt source code

The dbt project code was copied under the root directory in the container, under the path /dbt. The docker run command for this container looked as follows:

docker run --rm --env-file .env --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -w "/dbt" "${IMAGE_URI}" bash -c "dbt deps ${CI_PROFILE_TARGET} && dbt seed ${CI_PROFILE_TARGET} ${REFRESH:-"--full-refresh"}"

You can see that we removed the -v option which was used to mount the volume, and the working directory has been set to the path of the dbt project under the root directory.

  • When executing the above command, the container exits almost immediately, producing no output, with empty logs.
  • After playing a lot with the arguments of the run command, we figured out that the origin of the issue was the --user argument and how it interacts with dbt.
    • When running the container with different bash commands, such as ls, the container runs and exits successfuly without any issues.

Solution

We obviously realized that the --user argument was not needed any further, since its purpose was to enable the CI/CD user to delete files generated in the mounted volume. So removing it altogether fixed our issues.

docker run  --env-file .env -w "/dbt" "${IMAGE_URI}" bash -c " dbt deps ${CI_PROFILE_TARGET} && dbt seed ${CI_PROFILE_TARGET} ${REFRESH:-"--full-refresh"}
title: Docker container fails silently when running dbt commands with the wrong container user configuration
answer:
I think I see the issue. You said:

  • We set the user to have the same id and group id as the user running the docker run command.

While the '--user' sets the "user" to be used inside your container.

Example:

$ docker run -it node bash

root@7d6ee24e902d:/# whoami
root

while:

$ docker run --user 102 -it node bash

I have no name!@310bda9657c6:/$ whoami
whoami: cannot find name for user ID 102

As you can see, this changes my user inside the container, not the user who runs the docker command outside.
